strengths: The paper provides a clear and useful analysis of why weak-perspective camera models preclude metric shape and global translation estimation, and the pose ambiguity study in Sec. 3.2 (Fig. 4), showing PA-MPJPE can differ by up to 16.76mm across metrically plausible solutions, is a valuable empirical contribution in itself.

The camera ray map representation (Sec. 4.1) is an elegant and simple way to encode bounding box + intrinsics information; it is cropping-invariant and avoids CLIFF's ad-hoc bbox parameterization, and the ablation in Table 5 shows substantial gains (e.g., 3DPW PVE 129.2 -> 72.2) over directly feeding intrinsics.

The method is notably simple: a per-frame regressor with a ray encoder achieves trajectory estimation competitive with temporal methods that use SLAM/decoder modules (Tables 3-4), without temporal input or explicit 3D losses, which is an interesting and potentially useful finding.
Evaluation spans multiple settings (3DPW, EMBD-1/2, Human3.6M, qualitative COCO point-cloud overlays) and covers both known and estimated intrinsics, including a comparison under GT extrinsics.
Limitations (dependence on UniDepth failure cases) are explicitly acknowledged.
weaknesses: The claim of 'state-of-the-art performance' is overstated relative to the evidence. On local pose (Table 2) the method is clearly behind temporal baselines (3DPW PA-MPJPE 37.5 vs. 35.6/35.9 for TRAM/WHAM; EMBD-1 MPJPE 87.1 vs. 74.4/79.7). On trajectory (Table 3, EMDB-2), the method is actually slightly worse than TRAM w/ M.D. (WA-M 77.0 vs. 76.4; W-M 226.0 vs. 222.4); it only outperforms TRAM under GT extrinsics (61.3 vs. 62.7) and on static-camera Human3.6M. The text asserts the method 'slightly outperforms TRAM,' which Table 3 does not consistently support.

The core empirical claim that standard perspective projection with ray conditioning alone yields metric accuracy would be strengthened by isolating the effect of UniDepth: there is no ablation of sensitivity to focal-length/intrinsics estimation error, no comparison against simply feeding UniDepth-derived K into a CLIFF-style formulation with proper handling, and no breakdown between known- and unknown-intrinsics test data on EMDB.

The ablation study is thin: only two configurations (Bbox+K vs. Ray) are compared. There is no analysis of alternative ray encodings, robustness to noisy intrinsics, or the interaction between the ray conditioning and the pose ambiguity discussed in Sec. 3.2 - i.e., the analysis section motivates 'acceptable ambiguity' but the experiments do not quantify whether the network resolves it within that range.

Fairness of comparisons is unclear: the method is trained on 3DPW + Human3.6M + MPI-INF-3DPH and evaluated on datasets overlapping these training sets (3DPW, Human3.6M), while baseline training protocols (and whether baselines use the same UniDepth/intrinsics at test time) are not detailed; this complicates direct comparison with TRAM/WHAM numbers.
No code release or reproducibility statement is mentioned; given the reliance on a specific backbone (HMR2.0), UniDepth version, and training recipe, reproducibility is a concern.

Several writing issues reduce clarity: Section 3.1 mixes motivation and method details, Fig. 2/3 analysis is largely qualitative, and Table 1's 'No need' for 3D loss and trajectory module could be stated more precisely (the method still benefits from 3D-annotated training datasets via mimic/shape losses).

strengths: The paper provides a clear and well-motivated analysis (Sections 2-3) of why weak-perspective camera models used in prior HMR methods (e.g., HMR, SPIN, CLIFF) inherently cannot recover metric scale, including a quantitative demonstration of the depth/scale ambiguity (Fig. 4, PA-MPJPE up to 16.76mm across solutions). This analysis is a useful contribution in itself.

The proposed camera ray representation is elegant: encoding intrinsics and bounding-box information as a per-pixel ray map is crop-invariant and avoids the ad hoc parameterization issues the authors identify in CLIFF-style conditioning (Eq. 1 vs. Eqs. 3-4).

The method is simple: it requires no trajectory module, no temporal input, no 3D training supervision, and no extra metric-regularization networks, which is an attractive property relative to TRAM, WHAM, GVHMR, and TRACE.

Results are competitive: per-frame performance surpasses comparable per-frame baselines (CLIFF, HMR2.0, ReFit) on 3DPW and EMBD-1, and the trajectory results on EMBD-2 and Human3.6M are on par with or slightly better than TRAM under both estimated and GT camera extrinsics.
The qualitative 3D overlay with estimated point clouds (Fig. 8) is a compelling demonstration of metric-awareness on in-the-wild data.
weaknesses: Overclaiming relative to the evidence. The abstract and conclusion claim 'state-of-the-art performance, even compared with sequential-HMR methods,' but Table 2 shows the method is worse than the temporal methods TRAM and WHAM on all three metrics on both 3DPW and EMBD-1 (e.g., PA-MPJPE 37.5 vs. 35.6 TRAM / 35.9 WHAM on 3DPW; 52.4 vs. 45.7 TRAM on EMBD-1). The trajectory gains over TRAM in Tables 3 and 4 are marginal (e.g., WA-MPJPE 77.0 vs. 76.4 with masked-DROID on EMBD-2) and are not consistent across conditions. The paper quietly repositions this in Section 5.2 ('The specific difference is acceptable'), which conflicts with the headline claims.

Missing comparison with the most relevant competitor. The related work discusses BLADE [30], which also achieves metric HMR using DepthAnythingV2, but no quantitative comparison against it is reported. Given the paper's central claim of metric HMR, omitting this baseline significantly weakens the empirical case.

The 'metric shape' claim is not quantitatively evaluated. No shape-specific metric (e.g., per-subject height error or shape parameter consistency) is reported; the argument for metric shape rests largely on qualitative figures, even though Section 3.2 itself shows that metric shape and global translation are ambiguously traded off.

The core dependency on UniDepth is under-examined. The method's metric capability in the wild hinges on UniDepth's intrinsics estimate, yet there is no ablation or error analysis of sensitivity to intrinsics/focal-length errors, no failure-case analysis beyond one sentence in the limitations, and no comparison of UniDepth-predicted K vs. ground-truth K on the quantitative benchmarks.

The ablation study (Table 5) is minimal: only two configurations (CLIFF-style Bbox+K vs. Ray) on a single backbone. There is no ablation of the two-encoder (image vs. ray) architecture, no comparison against simply concatenating raw K parameters, and no analysis of robustness to inaccurate K, which is the paper's central design question.

The pose ambiguity analysis in Section 3.2 concludes that solutions 'can still reach 16.76mm' PA-MPJPE difference, which arguably undermines rather than supports the claim of accurate metric recovery; the paper does not clearly explain why its training procedure resolves this ambiguity better than prior work.

Novelty is moderate. Conditioning a regression network on ray maps or camera-geometric cues has appeared in related forms (UniDepth's ray maps, TRAM's use of true perspective projection with GT K, Zolly's focal-length-aware formulation), and the overall pipeline is a fairly direct combination of HMR2.0, UniDepth, and a ray-conditioned input.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, and key details (loss weighting, dataset mixing ratios, training data augmentation, how UniDepth intrinsics are fed during training on datasets with known K) are absent or vague.

strengths: The paper provides a clear and useful analysis of why weak-perspective camera models fundamentally limit metric shape/position estimation (Sec. 3, Figs. 2-4), including a quantitative illustration of pose ambiguity (PA-MPJPE differences up to 16.76mm across body-height solutions), which is a valuable contribution in itself.

The proposed camera-ray representation is simple, elegant, and well-motivated: it encodes intrinsics, bounding box, and image size in a unified, crop-invariant form, avoiding the three identified shortcomings of CLIFF-style conditioning (Eq. 1). The method requires no temporal input, no trajectory/SLAM module, and no 3D-loss supervision, making the pipeline notably simpler than TRAM/WHAM/GVHMR.

The ablation in Tab. 5 is convincing: replacing direct Bbox+K conditioning with the ray representation yields large gains (e.g., 3DPW MPJPE 111.5 -> 60.5, PVE 129.2 -> 72.2), directly supporting the central design claim.

Trajectory results are strong: the method is on par with or better than TRAM/WHAM on EMDB with both estimated and GT extrinsics (Tab. 3), better than TRAM on static-camera Human3.6M (Tab. 4), and qualitative point-cloud overlays (Fig. 8) support the metric 3D positioning claims.

The paper is honest in places: it acknowledges that the ambiguity analysis implies a 'reasonable' rather than unique metric solution, and states that slightly worse local pose than temporal methods is acceptable given no temporal information.
weaknesses: The abstract and conclusion overclaim: 'achieves state-of-the-art performance, even compared with sequential HMR methods, in metric pose, shape, and global translation.' Table 2 contradicts this for local pose: the method is clearly behind WHAM (37.5 vs 35.9 PA-MPJPE; 60.5 vs 57.8 MPJPE on 3DPW) and behind TRAM on EMDB-1 local metrics. SOTA holds mainly for trajectory, not for 'metric pose and shape'.

The central claim of metric SHAPE recovery is never quantitatively evaluated. No body-height error, no metric shape error, or comparison of estimated vs. GT subject scale is reported; Tab. 4 evaluates only WA-MPJPE/W-MPJPE/RTE/ERVE (joint/trajectory metrics). Given 'Metric' is the paper's headline contribution, this is a material gap in evidence.

Dependence on UniDepth for unknown intrinsics is a significant practical limitation that is under-examined. UniDepth's own metric scale accuracy limits the approach, no analysis of sensitivity to intrinsics/depth errors is provided, and the limitations section admits failure cases are simply not handled. Related metric-HMR work (BLADE [30]) is discussed in Sec. 2.2 but never compared against, despite being the closest single-image competitor.

The evaluation protocol for trajectory comparison (Tab. 3) raises fairness questions: the paper uses Masked-DROID for camera extrinsics while prior methods use DPVO or GT gyro; differences between SLAM backends could confound the comparison, and this is not ablated.

The ablation is thin: only two conditions (Bbox+K vs. Ray) with a single backbone. No exploration of alternative camera-conditioning designs, no results isolating the contribution of UniDepth-estimated intrinsics vs. GT intrinsics on the pose benchmarks, and no variance/significance reporting.

No code release or reproducibility statement is provided, and training data details (e.g., whether 3DPW/EMDB test subjects are excluded, intrinsics handling per dataset at train vs. test time) are insufficiently specified for independent reproduction.

Presentation issues: Table 1 is somewhat self-serving (e.g., 'No need' entries), Sec. 3.2's conclusion that the goal is a 'reasonable' rather than unique solution sits uneasily with the abstract's emphasis on accurate metric recovery, and the writing contains informal phrasing ('we are curious if there is a way...').

strengths: The paper presents a unified, single-frame framework (MetricHMSR) that recovers local pose, metric shape, and metric 3D position without task-specific modules, which is a meaningful system-level contribution in a field currently dominated by pipelines that bolt on trajectory/depth modules.

The pixel-aligned camera ray map is a clean way to jointly encode intrinsics and bounding-box information (generalizing CLIFF's bounding-box conditioning), and the supplementary material provides a clear motivating analysis (Fig. 9/10) of why focal length and principal point matter for metric depth and global position.

Empirical results are strong: best PA-MPJPE/MPJPE/PVE on 3DPW (33.6/53.0/62.7) and competitive global trajectory results on EMDB-2 and RICH, including the best RTE on RICH (1.9), achieved with per-frame processing rather than video input.
The human-guided metric depth refinement module is a sensible idea that exploits metric human meshes as scale anchors, and reported gains over MapAnything (AbsRel 0.18→0.13) support its usefulness.

The authors contribute a new synthetic zoom-varying dataset (SynFocal) addressing a real gap (existing datasets have fixed focal lengths), and the ablation (Table 6) shows both the ray representation and the MoE decoder contribute non-trivially (e.g., 3DPW MPJPE 57.2→55.0→53.0).
Analysis of expert routing (Figures 4, 5, 12, 13) goes beyond simply plugging in MoE, showing semantic specialization of experts across body parts and bounding-box scales.
weaknesses: The depth refinement evaluation is weakly supported: it is evaluated only on a self-defined 9:1 split of PROX with a non-standard protocol, MAE units are never specified, and the comparison numbers for Metric3D (AbsRel 0.76, δ1 = 0.01) appear erroneous or misconfigured, undermining confidence in Table 5. A standard depth benchmark or at least a sanity-checked baseline comparison is needed.

There is a circularity concern in the depth refinement: the metric anchors are derived from the method's own HMR mesh predictions, so errors in the mesh can propagate into the 'refined' depth; no analysis of this error coupling (e.g., performance with oracle vs. predicted meshes) is provided.

The ablation study is too coarse: it ablates only 'Image only / +Ray / +Ray & MoE' at the level of the full system. Key design choices (number of routed experts, shared expert, ray expert, Patch vs. Global MoE, soft MoE vs. standard MoE) are not ablated, so the specific MoE architecture claims are not substantiated.

SOTA claims are somewhat overstated: on EMDB-2 the method trails PromptHMR-vid (55.6 vs. 52.9 WA-MPJPE, 152.5 vs. 142.1 W-MPJPE), and on EMDB-1 it is second/third on most metrics; the paper is best framed as competitive rather than state-of-the-art.

The system depends on VGGT-estimated intrinsics when ground truth is unavailable, but no analysis of how intrinsic estimation error propagates to metric position accuracy is provided — this is central to the claimed robustness under varying intrinsics.

Novelty is incremental in places: camera-ray conditioning borrows directly from NeRF-style ray parameterization (and is close in spirit to PersPose's perspective encoding), and Soft MoE/shared experts are imported from the MoE literature with limited adaptation; the routing analysis, while interesting, is largely qualitative.

SynFocal robustness results are reported only against Human3R; other perspective-aware baselines (CameraHMR, PromptHMR, PersPose, CLIFF) that appear in the local-pose tables are absent from the varying-intrinsics comparison.
No runtime, parameter count, or memory comparison is given, making it hard to judge the practical cost of the dual-encoder + MoE design versus baselines like Human3R.

The manuscript has numerous presentation defects that hurt clarity: recurring grammatical errors ('We proposed', 'An specific designed HumanMoE network'), undefined notation at first use (K experts vs. N experts inconsistency in Eq. 3), Table 6 labeled EMDB-2 but containing WA-M./W-M. columns without clarifying predicted vs. GT extrinsics, and metric definitions (PRSD vs. RPSD) used inconsistently in Sec. 7.5/6.6.

strengths: Strong empirical results: best performance across all three metrics (PA-MPJPE 33.6, MPJPE 53.0, PVE 62.7) on 3DPW local pose estimation (Tab. 4), and best RTE among all methods on RICH (Tab. 3), achieved with a single-frame (online) model.

The pixel-aligned camera ray map is a reasonable and well-motivated representation that unifies bounding box and intrinsic information, directly addressing the crop/scale ambiguity problem identified in CLIFF; the ablation (Tab. 6) shows the ray input alone improves WA-MPJPE from 64.5 to 56.4 on EMDB-2.

Contribution of the SynFocal dataset fills a real gap (existing benchmarks use fixed focal lengths), and the RPSD comparison (1.1 cm vs. 21.6 cm for Human3R, Tab. 7) convincingly demonstrates robustness to focal length variation.

The human-guided depth refinement module is a sensible use of the metric mesh as a scale anchor, with clear quantitative gains over MapAnything (AbsRel 0.13 vs 0.18, Tab. 5), and the pseudo-annotation application to COCO/MPII/AIC is potentially useful to the community.
Broader coverage than many related works: the paper evaluates local pose, global trajectory, varying intrinsics, and depth estimation on multiple datasets (3DPW, EMDB-1/2, RICH, PROX, SynFocal).
weaknesses: Limited novelty in individual components: camera rays follow NeRF [29] and the formulation closely extends CLIFF [25] and PersPose [16]; the depth refinement is essentially a disparity-space affine correction applied on top of MapAnything [19], with intrinsics estimated by VGGT [43]. The core claimed contribution reduces largely to re-combining existing pieces, and the 'unified, no specialized modules' claim is undermined by the pipeline still depending on external models (VGGT, MapAnything).

The Human MoE motivation is overclaimed and under-supported. The central narrative of 'feature-level disentanglement' rests on qualitative routing heatmaps (Figs. 4-5) and descriptive statistics in the supplement; there is no rigorous analysis (e.g., expert ablations, controlled comparisons with a plain transformer at matched capacity/FLOPs, or evidence that expert specialization—rather than simply added parameters—causes the gains). The ablation in Tab. 6 has only three rows and cannot disentangle the ray encoder, MoE capacity increase, and routing design.

Evaluation breadth and fairness concerns: Table 2 (GT extrinsics) omits Human3R; several baselines have missing entries (ERVE for SLAHMR, PromptHMR-vid, Human3R); the depth refinement is evaluated only on the authors' own 9:1 split of PROX—a small dataset—raising overfitting and generalization questions; and on SynFocal the method is compared only against Human3R rather than the stronger baselines (PromptHMR, CameraHMR, TRAM) used elsewhere.

Some headline claims are overstated relative to the tables: on RICH the method's WA-MPJPE (109.6) is actually worse than WHAM (108.4) and roughly tied with Human3R (110.0); on EMDB-2 with GT extrinsics, PromptHMR-vid (52.9) outperforms the proposed method (55.6). 'State-of-the-art' framing in the abstract and conclusion does not consistently hold.

Clarity and polish are below the bar for publication: grammatical errors throughout ('We encodes 3D position', 'An specific designed HumanMoE', 'exisiting online methods', 'Build upon CUT3R'), loss weights λ are never specified, the ablation study section in the main text is a single sentence deferring everything to the supplement, and inconsistent terminology (PRSD vs RPSD, HMR 2.0 vs HMR). No code release is mentioned, which weakens reproducibility given the many training details deferred to the supplement.

The MoE loss design details (e.g., the λ in Eq. 4, the treatment of ray vs image tokens in load balancing) and the Global MoE analysis appear only in the supplement, so the main paper's methodological description is incomplete on its own.

strengths: Comprehensive benchmark coverage: the method is evaluated on local pose (3DPW, EMDB-1), global trajectory (EMDB-2, RICH), varying intrinsics (SynFocal), and metric depth (PROX), which is unusually thorough for an HMSR paper. It achieves the best results on 3DPW across all three metrics (Table 4), the best RTE on RICH among online and offline methods (Table 3), and matches offline video methods on EMDB-2 despite being a per-frame online method (Table 1).

The pixel-aligned camera ray map is a well-motivated conditioning mechanism: it unifies bounding-box and intrinsic information in a single representation that survives cropping/scaling (Eq. 1-2), addressing a concrete, previously identified problem (CLIFF's information-loss ambiguity). The supplementary analysis of focal length vs. metric depth (Fig. 9) and bbox vs. 3D position (Fig. 10) clearly motivates the design.

The ablation (Table 6) supports both main components: adding rays improves all metrics (e.g., EMDB-2 W-MPJPE 191.8 -> 154.1), and the Human MoE provides further gains (152.5). The routing analysis (Fig. 4 heatmap, Fig. 5 allocation maps, Figs. 12-13 on bbox scale) provides qualitative but plausible evidence that experts specialize by body part, foreground/background, and subject distance.

The robustness result under varying intrinsics is striking and well quantified: RPSD of 1.1 cm vs. 21.6 cm for Human3R and RDE of 0.10 vs. 0.14 (Table 7, Fig. 8), directly supporting the claim that explicit ray conditioning yields metric consistency under zoom.

The human-guided depth refinement module is a sensible use of the metric mesh as scale anchor, with a quantified improvement over MapAnything (MAE 0.58 -> 0.46 on PROX, Table 5), and it enables a practical byproduct (pseudo-GT depth for COCO/MPII/AIC).

The SynFocal dataset addresses a real gap: existing HMR benchmarks mostly have fixed focal lengths, so a zoom-varying synthetic benchmark with Blender/3D-FRONT/THuman renders is a useful community contribution.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely compositional rather than fundamental: camera rays follow NeRF [29] and CLIFF-style conditioning; Soft MoE [31], shared experts [10, 15], and the load-balancing loss (Eq. 4) are all established techniques applied essentially as-is. The 'Human MoE' and 'feature-level disentanglement' framing is supported only by qualitative routing visualizations; no experiment demonstrates that disentanglement (rather than extra capacity) is the causal source of the gains.

The ablation is thin for a paper whose central architectural claim is the MoE: only three configurations (image-only, +ray, +ray&MoE) are tested, on a single table. There are no ablations over the number of routed experts, the ray expert, shared vs. routed experts, Patch vs. Global MoE, the soft load-balancing loss, the over-complete losses (Eq. 5), or encoder choices (ViTPose + ViT-L), all of which are design decisions the paper advocates.

Results on EMDB-1 are not state of the art: MetricHMSR trails CameraHMR and PromptHMR on PA-MPJPE, MPJPE, and PVE (Table 4), and on EMDB-2 with GT extrinsics PromptHMR-vid outperforms it on WA-MPJPE and W-MPJPE (55.6/152.5 vs. 52.9/142.1, Table 2). The text's claims of 'state-of-the-art performance' are stronger than the tables in places; 'best overall performance' should be qualified.

The depth refinement evaluation uses a nonstandard 9:1 train/test split of PROX defined by the authors, and one baseline number (Metric3D: AbsRel 0.76, delta1 = 0.01) appears anomalous, undermining confidence in the depth comparison. Evaluation on a standard benchmark split would be considerably more convincing.

Dependence on estimated intrinsics via VGGT when GT intrinsics are unavailable is mentioned but never analyzed: there is no measurement of how intrinsic-estimation error propagates to metric position errors, which is central to the paper's core claim in the in-the-wild setting.

Writing and presentation quality need substantial revision: multiple grammatical errors ('We encodes 3D position', 'An specific designed HumanMoE', 'different patches varies'), inconsistent metric naming (RPSD vs. PRSD in Sec. 6.6), inconsistent figure/section referencing, and vague justification for design choices (e.g., the 'insights' in the introduction are asserted rather than argued).

Reproducibility is uncertain: no code or data release is stated, several hyperparameters (loss weights lambda, MoE load-balancing weight, number of MoE layers) are deferred to supplementary or unspecified, and the single-GPU, 40-epoch training recipe with ViT-L encoders suggests potentially heavy compute that is not characterized.
